hearts.tree/aetius-of-antioch: Aetius taught that the Son is unlike the Father, because only God is unbegotten, and his followers were called Anomoeans. Even many Arians found this too much, and the council of 360 gave him up, though Julian later recalled him and Eunomius carried the teaching on.
hearts.tree/alexander-of-alexandria: Alexander, bishop of Alexandria under Constantine, fell out with his priest Arius, put him out of the church and condemned his teaching, with Athanasius at his side at Nicaea.
hearts.tree/ammianus-marcellinus: Ammianus, a Greek-born former soldier who probably kept the old Roman faith, wrote a history of Rome to 378 and is valued as a largely fair outside witness who both mocked and praised the Christians.
hearts.tree/auxentius-of-durostorum: Auxentius, Ulfila's pupil and a bishop of the party called Arian, wrote a letter telling his teacher's life, which survives because Maximinus copied it into his own book.
hearts.tree/basil-of-caesarea: Basil turned from rhetoric to a life of prayer and service, wrote rules for monks living together, and built a great lodging for the poor and sick. As bishop he defended the Holy Spirit's place beside the Father and the Son, which a council declared after his death.
hearts.tree/conference-of-carthage-411: In 411 an imperial judge heard Catholic and Donatist bishops debate at Carthage which was the true church, ruled for the Catholics and banned Donatist meetings; the record comes mostly from the winning side.
hearts.tree/council-of-arles-314: Constantine called bishops to Arles in 314 to hear the Donatists' charge that Caecilian's ordination was worthless; they cleared him and made rules on Easter, rebaptism and clergy who handed over the Scriptures.
hearts.tree/council-of-ephesus-431: The council of Ephesus in 431, led by Cyril, deposed Nestorius over whether Mary could be called Mother of God, that is, how God and man are one in Christ. A rival assembly deposed Cyril, and the sides reunited in 433, while the Church of the East in Persia stood outside the verdict.
hearts.tree/council-of-sardica-343: The two emperors called a council at Sardica to settle the case of Athanasius and Marcellus; East and West split and condemned each other, and the West cleared both men and made rules for appeals to Rome.
hearts.tree/councils-of-ariminum-and-seleucia-3: Constantius II pressed the bishops, split between Ariminum and Seleucia, into one creed that called the Son like the Father and dropped the word "substance"; worn down, they gave way, and the world seemed to wake up Arian.
hearts.tree/didymus-the-blind: Didymus, blind from age four, became a famous teacher of the church's school at Alexandria, a defender of the Nicene faith and an admirer of Origen, for which he was later condemned.
hearts.tree/ephrem-the-syrian: Ephrem, a deacon of Edessa, taught the church's faith in hymns, answering rival teachers in the same meters their songs used, and in a famine ran the city's relief.
hearts.tree/epiphanius-of-salamis: Epiphanius, bishop of Salamis, wrote the Panarion, a medicine chest naming eighty heresies with a cure for each, and in old age fought Origen's followers in Jerusalem and Constantinople.
hearts.tree/eutyches: Eutyches confessed one nature in Christ after the union; for that he was condemned in 448, restored in 449 and condemned again at Chalcedon in 451, and both sides of the coming split cursed his name.
hearts.tree/eznik-of-kolb: Eznik, a pupil of Sahak and Mesrop, translated the Scriptures and wrote the Refutation of the Sects, taking apart the Persian magi's story of Zurvan; as bishop he answered a Persian edict.
hearts.tree/fabiola-of-rome: Fabiola, a noble Roman widow, did public penance, sold her property for the poor and founded a hospital where she nursed the sick herself, and studied Scripture with Jerome.
hearts.tree/first-council-of-constantinople-381: Theodosius called the council of 381 to establish the Nicene faith and give the capital a bishop; its creed declared the Holy Spirit worshipped and glorified with the Father and the Son, and Gregory of Nazianzus gave up his see there.
hearts.tree/frumentius: Frumentius, taken captive as a boy to the court of Aksum, gathered its Christians to pray and was made their bishop by Athanasius, tying the church of Aksum to Alexandria.
hearts.tree/germanus-of-auxerre: Germanus, a lawyer and governor made bishop of Auxerre, went to Britain against the Pelagian heresy and, in Constantius's saint's Life, led the Britons to an Alleluia victory.
hearts.tree/hilarion-of-gaza: Hilarion, Antony's disciple, is called the first monk in Palestine; known for healings, he fled the crowds his fame drew and wandered until he died on Cyprus.
hearts.tree/hilary-of-arles: Hilary, disciple and successor of Honoratus as bishop of Arles, clashed with Leo of Rome over the deposed bishop Celidonius and lost his power over the province of Vienne.
hearts.tree/honoratus-of-arles: Honoratus founded the monastery on the island of Lérins, drew Hilary and many others to it, and became bishop of Arles.
hearts.tree/john-cassian: Cassian carried the Egyptian desert's teaching into Latin for the West through his Institutes and Conferences, and his thirteenth Conference, on grace and free will, drew Prosper's attack.
hearts.tree/john-chrysostom: John Chrysostom preached plainly about the poor, and his blunt words to the powerful led to his exile and death; his followers who left the church over his fall came back only when his body came home.
hearts.tree/jovinian: Jovinian, a Roman monk known only through his opponents, wrote a book saying virgins, widows and wives are of equal merit, fasting is no better than eating, and all the baptized share one reward. Synods at Rome and Milan condemned it, and Jerome answered it at length.
hearts.tree/koriun: Koriun, a disciple of Mesrop Mashtots, wrote the Life of Mesrop and Sahak as an eyewitness and servant of those teachers. That Life is the main source for early Armenian literary history.
hearts.tree/liberius-of-rome: Liberius, bishop of Rome, refused the emperor Constantius's demand to condemn Athanasius and was exiled for it. Whether he later gave way in exile is disputed, and the people of Rome won his return.
hearts.tree/lucifer-of-cagliari: Lucifer of Cagliari refused to condemn Athanasius, was exiled and wrote fiercely against the emperor. Back from exile he made Paulinus bishop at Antioch, broke with Eusebius of Vercelli, and a strict Luciferian sect grew up around him.
hearts.tree/marcella-of-rome: Marcella, a noble Roman widow, was the first highborn lady at Rome to take up the monastic life openly, and became Jerome's partner in studying Scripture. She died after soldiers beat her when Rome was taken in 410.
hearts.tree/marcellus-of-ancyra: Marcellus of Ancyra, a Nicene bishop who wrote against Asterius, was accused of teaching that Christ's kingdom would end and that the Son began at his birth. He was deposed in the East and cleared in the West, and his orthodoxy stayed disputed.
hearts.tree/marius-mercator: Marius Mercator, a Latin writer living in Constantinople, warned the church there against the followers of Pelagius. He translated Nestorius into Latin so Latin readers would know and avoid his teaching.
hearts.tree/melania-the-elder: Melania the Elder, a Roman noblewoman widowed young, gave up her wealth, served the desert monks and founded a monastery at Jerusalem with Rufinus. Jerome first praised her and later cut her from his Chronicle.
hearts.tree/melitius-of-lycopolis: Melitius of Lycopolis split from Peter of Alexandria in prison over how to treat Christians who gave way under persecution, and ordained clergy on his own. His Church of the Martyrs lasted in Egypt for centuries, a split over church order rather than doctrine.
hearts.tree/mesrop-mashtots: Mesrop Mashtots made the Armenian letters so the faith could be preached and written in Armenian, and with Sahak began translating the Scriptures and founding schools. His pupils became the next Armenian writers.
hearts.tree/olympias-of-constantinople: Olympias, a wealthy widow and deaconess, gave her fortune to the poor and the churches and stood by John Chrysostom. She refused communion with his successor and was fined and driven from the city.
hearts.tree/ossius-of-cordoba: Ossius of Cordoba, an aged confessor and leading bishop at Nicaea and Sardica, told the emperor Constantius to stay out of church affairs. Held and tortured at Sirmium, he finally gave way, and at death bore witness to the force used on him.
hearts.tree/palladius-of-helenopolis: Palladius of Helenopolis, a monk who travelled to meet the desert holy men, wrote the Lausiac History about them. Made a bishop, he was caught up in the struggle over John Chrysostom.
hearts.tree/paula-of-rome: Paula, a Roman noblewoman, left her family after her husband's death, settled at Bethlehem and founded monasteries for men and women. She studied Scripture and Hebrew under Jerome's guidance.
hearts.tree/paulinus-of-milan: Paulinus of Milan, a member of Ambrose's household, wrote the Life of Ambrose at Augustine's request. As a deacon he also brought the charge against Caelestius at Carthage.
hearts.tree/pelagius: Pelagius, a British monk at Rome, taught that God made human nature able to choose the good and live without sin. He was cleared in Palestine, but Augustine and the African bishops, with Rome, condemned him over grace, and the sentence held.
hearts.tree/philostorgius: Philostorgius, a follower of Eunomius, wrote a twelve-book Church History from his party's side. It survives only through the hostile summary of Photius.
hearts.tree/possidius-of-calama: Possidius, bishop of Calama, lived beside Augustine for almost forty years, was with him at his death, and wrote his Life with a list of his books.
hearts.tree/priscillian: Priscillian, a Spanish layman turned bishop, called people to a strict life given wholly to God. Accused of heresy and sorcery by other bishops, he was tried before the emperor and put to death, and his followers honored him as a martyr.
hearts.tree/prosper-of-aquitaine: Prosper of Aquitaine defended Augustine's teaching on grace and God's choosing against the monks of Marseilles and John Cassian. He also kept a chronicle.
hearts.tree/rufinus-of-aquileia: Rufinus of Aquileia put Greek Christian books into Latin, above all Origen's First Principles and Eusebius's history. His softened Origen translation broke his old friendship with Jerome.
hearts.tree/socrates-of-constantinople: Socrates of Constantinople wrote a seven-book Church History carrying Eusebius's story on to 439, in a plain style and with a fairness that made some think him a Novatian.
hearts.tree/sozomen: Sozomen, an advocate from a Christian family near Gaza, wrote a Church History for the emperor Theodosius II, drawing heavily on Socrates without naming him.
hearts.tree/sulpicius-severus: Sulpicius Severus, a learned man from Aquitaine who gave up the world, wrote the Life of Martin of Tours, the Dialogues and a Chronicle ending with the trial of Priscillian.
hearts.tree/theodoret-of-cyrrhus: Theodoret was Antioch's leading fifth-century voice for Christ as one, God and man unmixed. He answered Cyril's twelve curses and stood by his deposed friend Nestorius. He was deposed in 449 and let back at Chalcedon only after cursing Nestorius. He was also a historian of the church and of the Syrian monks.
hearts.tree/tyconius: Tyconius was a Donatist who wrote the Book of Rules, seven keys for reading Scripture. He argued against his own party yet never joined the Catholics, and Augustine took up his rules while warning readers about him.
hearts.tree/ulfila: Ulfila was bishop of the Goths who led persecuted believers across the Danube, gave the Goths letters and the Scriptures in their own tongue, and taught them a Homoian creed that called the Son like the Father.
hearts.tree/agathias: Agathias of Myrina was a lawyer and poet who carried on Procopius's history. Church matters come in only in passing, and whether he was himself a Christian is disputed.
hearts.tree/augustine-of-canterbury: Augustine was the monk Gregory the Great sent to the English. He won over King Ethelbert of Kent, became the first archbishop of Canterbury, and failed to bring the British bishops under him.
hearts.tree/avitus-of-vienne: Avitus was bishop of Vienne who worked against the Arian church of the Burgundian court, wrote to Clovis on his baptism, and turned the heir Sigismund to the Catholic faith.
hearts.tree/barhadbeshabba-arbaya: Barhadbeshabba 'Arbaia, a Church of the East bishop of Halwan, wrote the Cause of the Foundation of the Schools, a history of God's schools from Adam to Edessa and Nisibis. He studied under the disputed teacher Henana.
hearts.tree/barsanuphius-and-john-of-gaza: Barsanuphius and John were two old men near Gaza who guided monks like Dorotheus through written questions and answers on humility, mourning and obedience.
hearts.tree/boethius: Boethius was a Roman senator who put Greek learning into Latin and wrote on the faith. He fell defending a fellow senator under Theodoric, and while condemned he wrote the Consolation of Philosophy before being killed.
hearts.tree/brendan-of-clonfert: Brendan founded the monastery of Clonfert. Adomnan glimpses him at Columba's Mass, but most of his story, above all the voyage to the Land of Promise, comes from Lives written centuries later.
hearts.tree/brigid-of-kildare: Brigid founded the monastery of Kildare, head of almost all the Irish churches. She is known mainly through Cogitosus's later Latin Life, which is mostly miracles.
hearts.tree/caesaria-of-arles-the-elder: Caesaria was the first abbess of the convent her brother Caesarius built at Arles. She is known almost wholly through his Life, and is often confused with the second Caesaria who followed her.
hearts.tree/caesarius-of-arles: Caesarius was bishop of Arles for forty years under Gothic kings. He spent the church's silver to free captives, defended his teaching on grace, and wrote rules and sermons for the wider church.
hearts.tree/cassiodorus: Cassiodorus was a Roman statesman who wrote for the Gothic kings, then founded the monastery of Vivarium and set his monks to read, study and copy books.
hearts.tree/ciaran-of-clonmacnois: Ciaran founded Clonmacnois and died young soon after. His story comes from the house's own late Life, with early writers confirming the man and his monastery.
hearts.tree/columbanus: Columbanus was an Irish monk who founded monasteries in Frankish Gaul and Lombard Italy, wrote a rule and a penitential, clashed with the Burgundian court, was driven out, and died at Bobbio.
hearts.tree/constantius-of-lyon: Constantius of Lyon was a fifth-century writer, friend of Sidonius, who wrote the Life of Germanus of Auxerre, a saint's Life to be used with care that Bede later copied.
hearts.tree/cosmas-indicopleustes: Cosmas was a merchant traveller turned monk who wrote the Christian Topography, picturing the world as a flat oblong under a vault modeled on Moses' tabernacle, and who witnessed churches as far as Ceylon and India.
hearts.tree/council-of-dvin-609: Abraham, head of the Armenian church, broke with the Georgian church head Kyrion after Kyrion accepted the Council of Chalcedon, and cursed him and his followers, by tradition at a synod in Dvin. The sources for the council itself are thin and late.
hearts.tree/cyril-of-scythopolis: Cyril of Scythopolis was a sixth-century monk who wrote the Lives of Sabas and Euthymius from the stories of desert elders, a prime source for the monks of Palestine, told from the side that accepted Chalcedon.
hearts.tree/david-of-wales: David was a British bishop and founder of monasteries who died around 600. Nearly all that is told of him comes from much later Lives, written partly to magnify the see of Saint David's.
hearts.tree/dionysius-exiguus: Dionysius Exiguus was a Scythian monk at Rome who translated Greek church canons into Latin and set out Easter tables that numbered the years from the Incarnation.
hearts.tree/dioscorus-of-alexandria: Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria after Cyril, presided at the council of 449 that deposed Flavian. He was himself deposed at Chalcedon in 451 and died in exile, held a defender of the true faith by the churches that rejected Chalcedon.
hearts.tree/dorotheus-of-gaza: Dorotheus of Gaza served the abbot John for nine years and wrote the Teachings, on cutting off one's own will, obedience and humility.
hearts.tree/elishe: Elishe wrote the History of the Armenian war, an eyewitness lament for Vardan's rising, which ended at Avarayr in 451, and for the Armenians' refusal of the Magi religion that Persia pressed on them. His life and later years come down to us in differing accounts.
hearts.tree/eugippius: Eugippius, abbot of the monastery at Severinus's tomb near Naples, wrote the Life of Severinus from the memories of the elder monks.
hearts.tree/euthymius-the-great: Euthymius, an Armenian-born monk in the Judean desert, known through Cyril's Life, healed and converted a Saracen chief's family. He accepted Chalcedon and brought the empress Eudocia back to it.
hearts.tree/evagrius-scholasticus: Evagrius, a lawyer of Antioch who lived through earthquake, fire and plague and served the patriarch Gregory, wrote a church history from the side that held to Chalcedon.
hearts.tree/faustus-of-riez: Faustus, abbot of Lérins and bishop of Riez, wrote On Grace. It argued for a middle way between Pelagius and strict predestination, and later writers argued over whether that made him a semi-Pelagian.
hearts.tree/ferrandus-of-carthage: Ferrandus, a deacon of Carthage, answered Rome's question on condemning the dead in the Three Chapters affair. He said a council's decisions should stand and that there is no good in fighting the dead. He also wrote to Fulgentius and may have written his Life.
hearts.tree/fulgentius-of-ruspe: Fulgentius, a Catholic bishop of Ruspe under the Arian Vandal kings, was twice exiled to Sardinia. He defended the Catholic faith before King Thrasamund and wrote, as a disciple of Augustine, on grace and predestination.
hearts.tree/gennadius-of-marseilles: Gennadius, a priest of Marseilles late in the fifth century, carried on Jerome's list of Christian writers and translated Greek works into Latin. Some readers see a semi-Pelagian slant in his work.
hearts.tree/gildas: Gildas, a sixth-century British churchman, wrote The Ruin of Britain, a sermon-letter attacking Britain's kings and clergy. Later writers read it to learn why the Britons lost their land.
hearts.tree/gregory-the-great: Gregory, a Roman noble who became a monk, was made pope in 590 against his will. He kept writing while he governed: the Moralia, the Pastoral Rule and the Dialogues.
hearts.tree/henana-of-adiabene: Henana, master of the school of Nisibis, was condemned for teaching that departed from Theodore of Mopsuestia, and the school split over him. He is known mostly through his opponents, against one pupil's praise.
hearts.tree/isidore-of-seville: Isidore, bishop of Seville for almost forty years, wrote the Etymologies, a gathering of nearly everything worth knowing, and led councils of the Spanish church.
hearts.tree/jacob-baradaeus: Jacob Baradaeus, a hunted bishop, travelled in secret across the East ordaining clergy. He built up the church that rejected Chalcedon, whose members came to be called Jacobites.
hearts.tree/john-climacus: John Climacus, a hermit and then abbot of Sinai, wrote the Ladder, thirty steps of the spiritual life from leaving the world to love.
hearts.tree/john-moschus: John Moschus, a monk of Palestine, wrote the Spiritual Meadow, stories of the monks of his time, for Sophronius. He wandered as the Persians advanced and died in Rome.
hearts.tree/john-of-beth-aphthonia: A John, superior of Beth Aphthonia, wrote a Life of Severus of Antioch in Greek, and who he was is disputed. He may be John bar Aphthonia, founder of Kenneshre and a leader of the bishops and monks who refused Chalcedon.
hearts.tree/john-of-biclaro: John, a Goth schooled in Constantinople, was exiled by the Arian king Leovigild. He founded the monastery of Biclaro, became bishop of Gerona and wrote a Chronicle of his own times.
hearts.tree/john-of-ephesus: John of Ephesus, a bishop and historian of the party that refused Chalcedon, converted thousands of pagans in Asia. He wrote the Lives of the Eastern Saints and a Church History from what he saw himself.
hearts.tree/john-rufus: John Rufus, an anti-Chalcedonian priest and later bishop of Maiuma, wrote the Plerophories, testimonies against the Council of Chalcedon drawn mostly from Peter the Iberian.
hearts.tree/joshua-the-stylite: Joshua the Stylite wrote a short Syriac chronicle of the famine, plague and war around Edessa about 500. He wrote so that the memory of the disasters would teach readers to repent.
hearts.tree/julian-missionary-to-the-nobadae: Julian, an old anti-Chalcedonian priest sent by Theodora, reached the Nobadae ahead of Justinian's envoy and converted their king and people to his own side's faith.
hearts.tree/justinian-i: Justinian, emperor from 527 to 565, made many church laws. He held priesthood and empire to be God's twin gifts and used the law and a council against dissenters.
hearts.tree/lazar-parpetsi: Lazar, an Armenian historian and Vahan Mamikonian's companion, wrote the third part of Armenia's annals at Vahan's order, after being accused, driven out and called back.
hearts.tree/leander-of-seville: Leander, bishop of Seville, is credited with turning the Visigoths from Arian teaching to the Catholic faith, which culminated at the Third Council of Toledo in 589. Gregory the Great was his friend.
hearts.tree/liberatus-of-carthage: A deacon of Carthage under Justinian who wrote the Breviarium, a short history of the quarrels over Nestorius and Eutyches, and who stood with the African defenders of the Three Chapters, sharing his bishop's exile.
hearts.tree/longinus-bishop-of-the-nobadae: An anti-Chalcedonian bishop who slipped away from watch in Constantinople and brought Christianity to the Nobadae and then the Alodaei beyond Egypt.
hearts.tree/mar-aba-i: A former magus who became catholicos of the Church of the East, ended its split between rival patriarchs and reformed marriage law, and suffered prison under the magi's hostility.
hearts.tree/marcellinus-comes: A Latin-speaking count from Illyricum who wrote at Constantinople a chronicle of the Eastern empire carrying on Eusebius and Jerome, hostile to heretics and warm to Justinian.
hearts.tree/marius-of-avenches: A Burgundian bishop of Avenches in the later 500s whose Chronicle carries on Prosper's, recording events of the Valais and Agaune.
hearts.tree/martin-of-braga: A Pannonian-born bishop who came to Galicia, helped turn the Sueves from Arian teaching to the Catholic faith, and wrote against the lingering pagan worship of country people.
hearts.tree/moses-of-khoren: A student of Sahak and Mesrop who wrote the History of Armenia, telling his nation's story to his teachers' deaths, though almost nothing precise is known of his life.
hearts.tree/peter-the-iberian: A Georgian prince raised as a hostage at the imperial court who became a monk and bishop of Maiuma, leading the monks near Gaza who refused Chalcedon.
hearts.tree/philoxenus-of-mabbug: An anti-Chalcedonian Syriac bishop of Mabbug who fought the teaching of two natures in Christ, helped drive out Flavian of Antioch, and died in exile at Gangra.
hearts.tree/primasius-of-hadrumetum: An African bishop who wrote five books on Revelation, and who, summoned to Constantinople over the Three Chapters, signed Vigilius's ruling but, by Victor's partisan account, later condemned them for gain.
hearts.tree/procopius-of-caesarea: A lawyer from Caesarea who served Belisarius and wrote the Wars, the Buildings and the Secret History, a historian of uncertain religion.
hearts.tree/reccared: The Visigothic king who, at the Third Council of Toledo, brought his Gothic people and the Sueves from Arian teaching into the Catholic faith.
hearts.tree/romanos-the-melodist: A Syrian deacon at Constantinople who, by the Menologion's story, received his gift of song from the Mother of God and wrote about a thousand kontakia, though almost nothing else is recorded of him.
hearts.tree/ruricius-of-limoges: A noble bishop of Limoges, drawn to the religious life by Faustus of Riez, known through two books of letters marked by frail health and humility.
hearts.tree/samson-of-dol: A British monk and bishop who founded Dol in Brittany, known mainly from an anonymous, disputed Life full of miracles that shaped later saints' Lives.
hearts.tree/second-council-of-constantinople-55: Justinian's council of 553 condemned the Three Chapters over Pope Vigilius's refusal, and Vigilius later gave way, leaving the council's standing disputed.
hearts.tree/severinus-of-noricum: An Eastern-come monk who guided the Danube towns of Noricum under barbarian raids, as his disciple Eugippius tells in a Life full of wonders.
hearts.tree/severus-of-antioch: An anti-Chalcedonian patriarch of Antioch who fled arrest under Justin, wrote from hiding in Egypt, and was condemned under Justinian.
hearts.tree/simeon-of-beth-arsham: A Persian bishop of the Syriac Orthodox side who spent his life debating the school of Nestorius and who reported the killing of the Christians of Najran.
hearts.tree/theodora-wife-of-justinian: Justinian's empress, painted as saint or scandal by opposing sources, who sheltered and championed the party that refused Chalcedon.
hearts.tree/theodosius-i-of-alexandria: The anti-Chalcedonian patriarch of Alexandria who spent most of his time in exile, refused the Tome of Leo even for an offered governorship, and gave his name to the Theodosians.
hearts.tree/theopistus: The deacon of Dioscorus who claims to have stayed with him from the summons to Chalcedon until his death in exile, and whose History survives only in a later reworked form.
hearts.tree/timothy-aelurus: An ascetic priest made anti-Chalcedonian bishop of Alexandria by the people, blamed for Proterius's death, exiled for many years and recalled by Basiliscus.
hearts.tree/venantius-fortunatus: An Italian poet who came to Gaul for love of Martin, settled at Poitiers near Radegund, wrote verse, saints' Lives and hymns such as Vexilla Regis, and became bishop.
hearts.tree/victor-of-tunnuna: Victor, a bishop in Roman Africa, defended the Three Chapters against the emperor Justinian and was beaten, imprisoned and held in monasteries for it. He wrote a partisan chronicle that tells his own sufferings and is prized for African church history.
hearts.tree/victor-of-vita: Victor of Vita wrote the History of the Persecution in Africa, a victim's polemic against the Arian Vandal kings Geiseric and Huneric, telling of exiles and mutilations of Catholics, some of which he lived through.
hearts.tree/vigilius-of-rome: Vigilius, made pope with imperial backing, was pressed by Justinian to condemn the Three Chapters; he wavered, first refusing in his Constitutum, then gave way, defending his change of mind by Augustine's example.
hearts.tree/zachariah-rhetor: Zachariah, a law student and advocate from Gaza, was the friend of Severus of Antioch; he wrote a Life to defend Severus and a church history attacking Chalcedon, and may later have become a Chalcedonian bishop of Mitylene.
hearts.tree/abbess-bugga: Bugga (Heaburg), an English abbess and daughter of Abbess Eangyth, was a lifelong friend and correspondent of Boniface who sent him gifts, sought his advice on going abroad, prayed at Rome and suffered troubles in old age.
hearts.tree/adam-jingjing: Adam (Jingjing), a priest of the Church of the East in Tang China, composed the Chinese text of the Xi'an stele of 781, setting out his church's faith in Chinese words and its history in China.
hearts.tree/adomnan-of-iona: Adomnán, abbot of Iona, wrote the Life of Columba and a book on the holy places; he came to accept the Roman Easter, won many in Ireland to it but not his own monks, and his rule protected women.
hearts.tree/agathon-of-alexandria: Agathon, a Coptic priest of Alexandria, secretly ministered to hidden believers disguised as a carpenter, later became patriarch, freed captives, and endured Theodore's persecution while praying for him.
hearts.tree/aidan-of-lindisfarne: Aidan, an Iona monk, was sent as bishop to Northumbria, taught the English gently and lived as he taught, giving to the poor and freeing slaves, while keeping the Irish Easter.
hearts.tree/al-baladhuri: Al-Baladhuri, a ninth-century Muslim historian, wrote the Futuh al-Buldan on the conquests, recording the fate of Saint John's church in Damascus and the terms given Christians; he is careful with sources but scarcely judges them.
hearts.tree/alcuin-of-york: Alcuin, master of the school at York, went to Charlemagne's court, taught the king, defended the faith against Felix of Urgel's Adoptionism, and became abbot of Saint Martin's at Tours.
hearts.tree/alexander-ii-of-alexandria: Alexander II, Coptic patriarch under Umayyad governors, was held for money, robbed of church vessels and threatened with branding; he begged to pay, refused the brand, and died.
hearts.tree/antony-of-choziba: Antony, a monk of Choziba, wrote the Life of his teacher George, telling how George kept him in the monastery, guided him through temptation and lived through the Persian invasion.
hearts.tree/athanasios-the-athonite: Athanasios, a monk on Athos, built the Great Lavra at Nikephoros Phokas's request, rebuked him for breaking his promise, made the house self-governing, and his rule became the standard for Athos.
hearts.tree/bede-of-jarrow: Bede, monk and priest of Wearmouth and Jarrow, gave his life to learning, teaching and writing, above all his History, and died dictating to the last.
hearts.tree/benjamin-i-of-alexandria: Benjamin I, Coptic patriarch, fled and hid for years when Heraclius tried to force Chalcedon on Egypt, returned under 'Amr's protection, and won back his people by gentleness.
hearts.tree/beuno: Beuno, a Welsh clergyman known from a late Life, founded churches on land given by kings, fled the English advance, and is credited with miracles and the house at Clynog Fawr.
hearts.tree/boniface-of-mainz: Boniface, an English monk, became missionary to the Germans and reformer of the Frankish church under papal and Carolingian backing, and was martyred in Frisia.
hearts.tree/braulio-of-zaragoza: Braulio, bishop of Zaragoza, was Isidore's friend and editor, and defended the Spanish bishops' gentler way with Jews against the pope's rebuke.
hearts.tree/cedd-and-chad: The brothers Cedd and Chad were humble bishops: Cedd preached to the East Saxons and founded Lastingham, and Chad, after yielding York, became bishop of the Mercians at Lichfield.
hearts.tree/cogitosus: Cogitosus wrote a Latin Life of Brigid of Kildare that describes her church and makes her house the head of the Irish churches; his date is disputed.
hearts.tree/cuthbert-of-lindisfarne: Cuthbert, a shepherd turned monk, became a hermit on Farne and a reluctant bishop of Lindisfarne, and was honored as a saint whose body was found whole.
hearts.tree/dionysius-of-tel-mahre: Dionysius, Syriac Orthodox patriarch under the caliphs, defended his church's rights and people before rulers, and wrote a history lamenting the suffering of Christians.
hearts.tree/eadburga-of-thanet: Eadburga, abbess of Thanet, known only from letters to and about her, supported Boniface with books and prayers and taught Leoba the art of verse.
hearts.tree/elias-of-nisibis: Elias, metropolitan of Nisibis in the Church of the East, wrote a year-by-year Chronography that names its sources, and he stood against a catholicos who bought his office.
hearts.tree/elipandus-of-toledo-and-felix-of-ur: Two Spanish bishops held that Christ in his humanity was adoptive Son. The Franks and Rome condemned this as heresy, and the two men held to it to the end.
hearts.tree/gregory-of-narek: Gregory, a tenth-century Armenian monk and abbot of Narek, wrote the book of prayers called Narek, still used in the liturgy and in private prayer.
hearts.tree/heraclius: Emperor Heraclius brought the holy Cross back to Jerusalem, and his name stood on the Ecthesis, a statement on Christ's operation that he later disowned and the Lateran council anathematized.
hearts.tree/hincmar-of-reims: Hincmar, archbishop of Reims and keeper of the Frankish annals, was a learned churchman who fought a long, bitter battle with his nephew, the bishop of Laon.
hearts.tree/humbert-of-silva-candida: Humbert led the papal envoys who laid an excommunication on the altar of Hagia Sophia in 1054, an act later read as completing the split between the churches.
hearts.tree/ildefonsus-of-toledo: Ildefonsus ran away to be a monk, became abbot of Agali and then bishop of Toledo, and wrote on the Virginity of Mary and on the famous writers of his church.
hearts.tree/isaac-of-alexandria: Isaac, a desert monk trained as a secretary, became Coptic patriarch of Alexandria by the Amir's order and survived the Amir's anger.
hearts.tree/jacob-of-edessa: Jacob of Edessa, a Syriac Orthodox scholar-bishop, burned the book of canons in protest when church leaders ignored them, and spent his life on Greek learning, grammar, chronicle and the correction of Scripture.
hearts.tree/john-iii-of-samannud: John III, Coptic patriarch, refused under torture to pay a ransom he could not pay, and rebuilt Saint Mark's and fed the poor through famine.
hearts.tree/john-of-nikiu: John, Coptic bishop of Nikiu, wrote a chronicle of the Arab conquest of Egypt and was deposed for a punishment that went too far.
hearts.tree/jonas-of-bobbio: Jonas, a monk and later abbot of Bobbio, wrote the Life of Columbanus from the accounts of those who knew him, along with other saints' Lives.
hearts.tree/joseph-i-of-alexandria: Joseph, a monk seized against his will to be Coptic patriarch, led his church through the Bashmurite revolt and faced rebuke and plots against his life.
hearts.tree/julian-of-toledo: Julian, bishop of Toledo, wrote the Prognosticon on the fate of souls, wrote against the Jews at the king's command, and led councils of Toledo.
hearts.tree/leoba: Leoba, an eighth-century English nun and kinswoman of Boniface, wrote to him in letter and verse and later served his mission as abbess in Germany.
hearts.tree/martin-i-of-rome: Pope Martin I held a synod that condemned the teaching of one will in Christ, and for that was seized, tried as a rebel and exiled to die at Cherson.
hearts.tree/maximus-the-confessor: Maximus the Confessor held that Christ has two wills and two workings, refused communion on the emperor's terms, and was mutilated and exiled for it.
hearts.tree/michael-i-of-alexandria: Michael I, Coptic patriarch, was jailed, beaten and threatened with death by Muslim rulers and stood firm, remembered as a martyr who shed no blood.
hearts.tree/moses-bar-kepha: Moses bar Kepha, a Syriac Orthodox bishop and commentator on Scripture, wrote a clear, ordered book on paradise and other works read in the church.
hearts.tree/muirchu: Muirchu wrote the oldest surviving Life of Patrick, at a bishop's command, likely as a tribute from Leinster to Armagh.
hearts.tree/nennius: The Historia Brittonum, a disputed history of the Britons given to Nennius, gathers annals and traditions from Adam to the English kings, including Arthur's battles.
hearts.tree/niketas-stethatos: Niketas Stethatos, a Studite monk and disciple of Symeon the New Theologian, wrote on tears, humility and prayer, and condemned his own book against the Latins in 1054.
hearts.tree/paul-the-deacon: Paul the Deacon, a Lombard monk of Monte Cassino who served at Charlemagne's court, wrote the History of the Lombards.
hearts.tree/paulus-emeritanus: Paul, a deacon of Mérida, wrote the Lives of the Fathers of Mérida, telling of its visions and of its bishops, above all Masona against the Arian king.
hearts.tree/photius-of-constantinople: A brilliant lay scholar raised in six days to patriarch of Constantinople, Photius clashed with Rome over his elevation and over the Latins' addition to the Creed, and was condemned, deposed, restored and finally sent away.
hearts.tree/pisentius-of-coptos-and-john-the-el: Pisentius, a reluctant ascetic bishop of Coptos who gave everything to the poor and hid from the Persians, is remembered through the Life his disciple and servant John wrote and witnessed.
hearts.tree/prudentius-of-troyes: Prudentius, a Spanish-born bishop of Troyes, kept the Annals of Saint-Bertin and defended double predestination against Hincmar of Reims, who later painted him as a defender of heresy.
hearts.tree/sebeos: Sebeos, a seventh-century Armenian bishop, wrote the History of Heraclius, the only Armenian account of the first Arab invasions, which he saw as a judgment for sin.
hearts.tree/severus-ibn-al-muqaffa: Severus, a Coptic bishop famed for his Arabic, is joined to the History of the Patriarchs of Alexandria, whose Coptic and Greek histories he had translated into Arabic for Egyptians who no longer knew those tongues.
hearts.tree/simon-i-of-alexandria: Simon, a Syrian chosen as Coptic patriarch (689 to 701), forgave the priests who poisoned him and held to the truth before the Amir when accused over a bishop for India.
hearts.tree/sophronius-of-jerusalem: Sophronius, a monk who became patriarch of Jerusalem, opposed the teaching that Christ had one operation, faced the Arab conquest of the city, and was vindicated by the Third Council of Constantinople.
hearts.tree/symeon-the-new-theologian: Symeon, a monk and abbot of Constantinople around 1000, taught that the soul can see God as light, and was exiled and recalled over the feast he kept for his teacher.
hearts.tree/theodore-of-tarsus: Theodore, a learned Greek monk from Tarsus, became archbishop of Canterbury at sixty-six and was the first archbishop the whole English church obeyed, ordering it through the Synod of Hertford.
hearts.tree/thomas-of-marga: Thomas, a monk of Beth 'Abhe who rose to bishop and metropolitan, gathered the stories of its holy men from named witnesses into the Book of Governors.
hearts.tree/tirechan: Tirechan, an Irish bishop and pupil of Ultan, wrote notes following Patrick from place to place to record the churches that belonged to Armagh.
hearts.tree/wilfrid-of-ripon: Wilfrid, bishop of York, championed Roman ways at Whitby and was driven from his see again and again, appealing to Rome each time.
hearts.tree/willibrord: Willibrord, a Northumbrian monk, became archbishop of the Frisians, preached among the pagans, and founded Echternach.
hearts.tree/yahya-ibn-said-of-antioch: Yahya, an eleventh-century Arab Christian historian, continued Sa'id ibn Bitriq's history and twice revised it as new chronicles reached him.
hearts.tree/bonaventure: Bonaventure, minister general of the Franciscans and later cardinal, wrote the Life of Francis meant to replace earlier Lives, and died at the Council of Lyon.
hearts.tree/gregory-vii: Gregory VII, pope from 1073 to 1085, claimed the pope's power to depose emperors, stripped Henry IV of his kingdoms, and received his penance at Canossa.
hearts.tree/innocent-iii: Innocent III held that royal power takes its light from papal authority as the moon from the sun, approved Francis's way of life, and held the Fourth Lateran Council.
hearts.tree/hugo-grotius: Grotius, a Remonstrant jurist, wrote a 1617 treatise defending Christ's death as satisfying divine justice against Socinus, and shared the ban on the Arminians after Dort.
hearts.tree/ignatius-of-loyola: Ignatius, a soldier converted while recovering from a wound, became a pilgrim and student, and with his companions founded the Society approved by Paul III in 1540.
